one_liner: Linux kernel module for Homa, a message-based datacenter RPC transport with far lower short-message tail latency than TCP.
what_it_does: Adds a new IP transport protocol (IPPROTO_HOMA, IANA number 146) to Linux as a loadable module, homa.ko. Homa is connectionless and message-oriented. One socket can have many concurrent RPCs to any number of peers and can also act as a server. Delivery is reliable and at-most-once. Apps open socket(AF_INET/AF_INET6, SOCK_DGRAM, IPPROTO_HOMA) and call sendmsg/recvmsg, passing Homa-specific control structs (homa_sendmsg_args, homa_recvmsg_args) and a receive-buffer region registered in advance with SO_HOMA_RCVBUF. It is a new API, not a replacement for TCP sockets.
how_it_is_fast: Receiver-driven flow control: a sender sends the first rtt_bytes of a message without asking, then sends more only when the receiver grants it. Receivers approximate SRPT (shortest remaining processing time first) with a bounded degree of overcommitment. Priorities are set through 8 switch priority queues keyed on DSCP bits, and a homa_prio daemon sets unscheduled-priority cutoffs from observed message sizes. A sender-side pacer/homa_qdisc keeps NIC queues short so small messages never wait behind large ones, and message framing removes TCP's head-of-line blocking. On the host side the ATC'21 paper credits most of the 100-byte RTT gain to busy-polling in recvmsg (~4 us) and SoftIRQ core selection (3-4 us), and higher RPC rate to GRO batching across RPCs.
when_to_use: Datacenter request/response traffic where P99 latency of short messages (hundreds of bytes to a few KB) under 50-80% network load is what hurts, e.g. fan-out services and storage/cache RPC.
Mixed workloads with both short and long messages (the Montazeri W3-W5 shapes), where TCP's per-stream head-of-line blocking and switch queue buildup inflate tail latency.
Highly connected clusters: one Homa socket reaches every peer, and the paper puts per-peer state at about 200 bytes versus about 2000 bytes per open TCP socket.

You control the whole stack: Linux 6.17.8 (main) or RHEL 8/9.5 (branches) hosts, Mellanox ConnectX-4/5/6 or Intel E810 NICs, and top-of-rack switches you can configure for DSCP strict-priority queues.
Transport research or benchmarking: the repo ships the cp_node/cp_vs_tcp/cp_bench harness, timetrace tools and /proc/net/homa_metrics used to produce its published numbers.
when_not_to_use: Bulk or single-stream throughput. In the paper's Table 2, one client doing 500 KB RPCs gets 10.0 Gbps versus 20.3 Gbps for TCP. Messages are capped at HOMA_MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH = 1,000,000 bytes, so large transfers must be chunked.
WAN or cross-datacenter links. The homa(7) man page says Homa is for RTTs of a few tens of microseconds and is not suitable for wide-area use.

Anywhere you cannot load an out-of-tree kernel module or configure switches: managed cloud VMs, unprivileged containers, macOS and Windows. Upstream Linux does not include it (no net/homa in mainline as of v7.3-rc4).

CPU-bound small-RPC servers. In the paper, 1.6 Mops/s used about 18 of 20 hyperthreads (~0.1 M req/s/core, versus ~10 M for kernel-bypass eRPC), and perf.txt (Sep 2025) says receive polling costs an extra 2-3 cores.

Hosts carrying heavy TCP traffic at the same time, or needing encryption. perf.txt (Jan 2026) shows Homa's short-message P99 rising about 4x when it shares hosts with TCP, and still about 30% worse with homa_qdisc. There is no TLS layer (grpc_homa supports only insecure channels).

integration.dependencies: Kernel build tree/headers that match the running kernel (main: Linux 6.17.8; rhel8 and rhel9.5 branches; older linux_x.y branches are stale), a kernel built with IPv6 (Kconfig depends on IPV6), and root for insmod. The homa_prio user-space daemon (util/) is recommended. Full performance also needs switch priority queues, jumbo frames, and NIC TSO for Homa packets (Mellanox) or TCP hijacking. The optional C++ homa::receiver helper and homa.h UAPI header ship in the repo.
integration.min_toolchain: Module is built with kbuild and the kernel's own compiler/flags (no GCC version documented). util/ tools and homa_receiver.cc need g++ with -std=c++17.
integration.platforms: Linux only. Tested on x86-64 (Intel xl170/c6620 and AMD c6525 CloudLab nodes per perf.txt); other architectures not documented. Verified NICs: Mellanox ConnectX-4/5/6 and Intel E810.
integration.thread_safety: Multiple threads may use one socket: the man page describes several threads blocked on a socket, and cp_node runs several receiver/server threads per socket. The C++ homa::receiver helper is explicitly not thread-safe per instance. Processes can share a socket only if they map its receive-buffer region at the same virtual address.

gotchas: Out of the box, performance is poor until the host and network are tuned. That means jumbo frames, NIC interrupt coalescing off, RPS on and RFS off, homa_qdisc configured on each tx queue, switch DSCP priority mapping, and TSO. INSTALL.md says software GSO is 'temporarily broken', so on NICs that won't segment Homa packets the fallback is TCP hijacking. Hijacked packets masquerade as TCP and can be dropped by datacenter switch filters.

The API has changed repeatedly. Homa 2.0 (Dec 2022) moved to sendmsg/recvmsg with an app-supplied mmap'd buffer pool. homa_send/homa_recv/homa_reply were removed in May 2025, private-RPC flags changed in Mar 2025, and since Feb 2025 unbound sockets reject incoming requests. Netdev review is expected to change the API again.

Receive buffers are registered up front (page-aligned region, 'tens of MB'). recvmsg returns ENOMEM when the pool is exhausted, and bpages are only returned to Homa on the next recvmsg. Raising the 1 MB message cap means editing a static_assert and recompiling every app (issue #48).

The upstream series (v20, posted 2026-09-14) is stripped to about 8,000 of 20,000 lines, and its cover letter says its performance is 'about the same as TCP'. The fast paths (grant scheduling, qdisc, hijack, GRO offload) exist only in this out-of-tree repo. notes.txt also records grant 'stranding' under very high load in large clusters, capping throughput at about 60-70% of link bandwidth. One rtt_bytes value is used for all peers, and the SIGCOMM incast optimization is not implemented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick HomaModule when tail latency of short RPCs under heavy network load is the problem and you can change host kernels and switch config. brpc, Kitex and rpcx win on QPS in user space but still run over TCP, so they keep its head-of-line blocking and congestion tails. grpc_homa is only a gRPC shim on top of this module, and its README says it has been unmaintained since late 2023 (gRPC 1.57, insecure channels only). Use it only if you must keep gRPC's API.
verified_claims_summary: The USENIX ATC'21 paper compared this module (2021 code, Linux 5.4.80, MTU 3000) with Linux kernel TCP (TCP_NODELAY, per issue #51 and cp_node.cc) and DCTCP (ECN threshold 70 KB) on 40 CloudLab xl170 nodes (Xeon E5-2640v4, ConnectX-4 25 Gbps, one Mellanox 2410 switch). Under high load on workloads W2-W5, short-message P99 was 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP, and P50 was 3.5-7.5x and 2.7-3.8x lower. Best-case 100-byte RTT was 15.1 vs 23.4/24.1 us, and RPC rate was 1.6 vs 1.0 Mops/s. No compiler version or flags are stated. The author's unreviewed perf.txt log (Jan 2026, current code, 100 Gbps c6620, W4 at 80 Gbps) still shows short-message P99 of about 91-99 us for Homa versus 833-1272 us for TCP.
status_note: Actively maintained by John Ousterhout (last commit 2026-09-25, upstreaming in progress on netdev). BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+ via per-file SPDX headers, so it is copyable, but it is an out-of-tree kernel module that must be rebuilt and ported for each kernel version it runs on.
